messages.subject: Multi-species sampling
parts:
Hello-
I am conducting surveys of birds in urban parks using line transects. I am
particularly interested in guild composition in the parks, as the parks
vary considerably in amount of forest habitat, density of both overstory
and understory, amount of shrub habitat, etc. as well as in area. I was
hoping to compare composition and density for several guilds across parks
by summing individual species=92 density estimates within a guild, for
example, ground nesters, in each park. However, for several species, our
sample sizes are too small to obtain reliable species-level density
estimates. I am wondering about calculating densities for multiple species
within a guild, as indicated in the 2001 book on page 301-302. Could I
group several species with similar detectabilities that occur in the same
guild and calculate an overall density estimate for the group? What should
I do if some species are absent from that guild in some of the parks (due
to area or habitat patch size, for example)? Thanks!

Yes, if you pool across species, you should still get a valid estimate of
overall density - provided each individual species satisfies the
assumptions of line transect sampling. Differences in detectability
between species do not invalidate this overall density estimate, but they
DO generate bias in density estimates by species, if you assume a common
detection function - more detectable species will be overestimated, and
less detectable species underestimated. I'm not sure why it should be a
problem if some species from within a guild are absent from some parks.
They clearly contribute zero density in those parks - both in terms of
true density and in terms of estimated density.

Steve Buckland
